Nextwave · Private briefing · August 2026

Where the R&D is going: NextOS Family

NextOS is Nextwave's AI operating system for small business. Family is its second track, and it is really one product: a tutor for your child that knows your child. It reads the school's emails, newsletters, portals and reports, works out what your child is actually being taught and where they are actually stuck, and turns that into a short illustrated lesson every morning. Built and used on one real family, mine, every day. Everything below is live product. Names, faces and schools are blurred out.

The pitch in four sentences

Every parent knows they should sit down and do homework with their kid, and almost none of them have the hour. So we built the thing that does it: an assistant that reads every school communication a family gets, lines it up against the year level the child is actually in, and produces a six-to-fifteen question morning session built from that week's real material. The questions are illustrated, read aloud, written by hand with a pen, and personalised down to the child's own cat, their sport, their friends and the trip they took last month, because a child will do a quiz about their own life and will not do a worksheet. Underneath it sits the household layer that got us here: two school inboxes swept daily, and one screen with the whole family's week on it.

1 · The household layer

Start with the boring part, because it is the part that earns the trust. One page, four people, the week ahead, and a live count of what each school needs from a parent. This is the screen the family opens on a phone at breakfast.

The family week: two children, two parents, and what school needs from you today.

2 · The school sweep

Two children at two different schools means two newsletter streams, two parent portals and a constant drip of notices. The bench sweeps both every morning at about half past five, reads everything, and splits it into what needs a decision and what is just news. This week it read nine messages and flagged five. Nothing here is typed in by hand.

The School Board, swept daily. Nine messages read, five need you, nothing slipped.

The same signal split per child into School, Sport, Health and Activities, with honest empty states.

3 · What the school signal is actually for

Everything above exists to feed this. The morning quiz is the product. It is a tutor that already knows what your child is being taught, because it read the school's own communications to find out, and it knows where they are stuck, because a teacher wrote it down and we caught it.

Fifteen questions, mapped to the child's real year level in the Australian curriculum, in eleven different question shapes so a week does not feel like the same worksheet five times. Every question is illustrated and read aloud in a real voice.

A live card. Illustrated, read aloud, and written about a trip this child actually took.

It is about their life, not a stock photo of a child

The engine holds a profile per child: their sport and their team, their friends' names, their hobbies, the town they live in, and their pets. Every set carries exactly one card about the family's own cats. Nine-year-olds do not do worksheets. They do answer questions about their cat.

The family's actual ragdoll cat, drawn into a division question about his food bowl.

They write it, with a pen

Spelling is not multiple choice, because spelling is not multiple choice at school. The child hears the word, traces it, then writes it freehand with a finger or an Apple Pencil, and handwriting recognition marks it. The word list is the teacher's own, taken straight off the school portal. The illustration behind it carries real handwriting too.

Trace, then write. The word list came from the child's teacher, not from us.

Live ink on the pad. Recognition marks the attempt, and only a first-time-correct word counts.

Times tables get their own round

Recall drills need a different feel to comprehension questions, so they got one: pop the cloud carrying the right answer, twelve in a row, streak counted.

The cloud round: rote recall, built as a game rather than a list.

And more formats are prototyped

Five further card shapes are built and playable in prototype, aimed at the moves a quiz cannot reach: recognition under a slow reveal, estimation, matching, placing a value on a line, and classification. These are labelled mockups, not shipped.

Zoom Reveal: the picture resolves over sixteen seconds; call it as early as you dare.

Bucket Sort: drag each number home. Tests classification, which recall questions cannot.

4 · Where the material comes from

Emails and portals are the automatic half. The other half is the parent pointing a camera at something: a school report, an assessment sheet, a page of homework, a note that came home in a bag. It gets read, filed, and turned into next week's questions.

Upload, paste or photograph. Reports and homework go in the same door.

5 · The loop, closed

Here is the whole thesis in one card. The teacher flags a spelling problem through the school portal. The bench reads it, works out what it means, and puts one card a day from that teacher's own word list into the child's quiz the next morning. The parent taps once. That is the hour of homework they did not have, done.

School signal in, lesson out, one tap of parental consent in between.

6 · The reason they come back

A tutor nobody opens is worth nothing, so the learning is wrapped in something a child wants to open. Each child gets a weekly magazine about their own week, illustrated with them in it, which is also the door into the morning quiz.

The child's own weekly magazine. Their week, their cat, their bracelet club.

And a five-day story to chase

The Morning Edition runs a week-long mystery: a thief called JADE, one clue a day, five countries. Answering the clue is answering a geography question. The morning quiz sits inside it as "your morning five is ready".

Monday's front page. The quiz is a panel in the paper, not a chore on a list.

Clue one. The companion answers questions about the world, so a curious child can keep pulling.

The companion they pick and keep

On first run the child hatches a companion and names it. It is the voice that walks them through the questions and the thing that makes the streak matter.

Five families, three names each, hatched once and kept.

Which lands back on their own page

All of it hangs off a page the child runs themselves: their week, the chore they are on, their pocket money, and two buttons, quiz and magazine.

The child's own page. No parent required to operate it.

7 · It talks

Voice as well as screen, on the phone the family already carries. It reads the questions aloud, and a parent can just ask it what they have forgotten this week.

The household assistant, live on voice.

Why this is an asset, not a burn

  • It is the same platform, pointed somewhere else. The bench, the voice layer, the decision cards, the hosting and the app shell were all built and paid for by the commercial track. What is genuinely new here is the school sweep, the learning engine and the illustration pipeline.
  • No new paid feeds. It reads the school communications the family already receives. Marginal cost for a second household is hosting and AI compute, not development.
  • The category is real, but split in three. Cozi sells the shared family calendar. Compass Education sells schools the parent portal that our sweep reads. 3P Learning, an Australian listed company, sells Mathletics and Reading Eggs. Three purchases, three logins, and not one of them joins what the school actually sent this week to what the child practises tomorrow morning. That join is the product, and it is the part that cannot be bought off a shelf.
  • The buyer is a guilty parent, not a keen one. We are not selling extra work to families who already do an hour of homework a night. We are selling that hour back to the ones who cannot find it.
  • Honest run cost. Hosting and AI compute, monthly, cancellable, nothing locked in.

The proof gate and the next 90 days

There is one measurement that counts, and it is not ours. One child's school runs a cumulative spelling review, seventy-five items, once a term. Term 1 was 42 out of 75. End of Term 2 was 57 out of 75, which is 56% up to 76%. The morning quiz was running for the whole of that gain, using that teacher's own word list.

What we will not claim: that the quiz caused it. There is no control, the child has a good teacher, and a term is a term. The claim that survives scrutiny is that it was running the whole time she improved, and that is enough to keep going on.

  • The Term 3 review, same seventy-five item instrument, same teacher. Using the school's own metric rather than one we invented is the entire point. That is the gate.
  • Then package it: a per-household subscription sold on the tutoring, with the school sweep as the reason it knows anything.
  • Then, and only then, the invest-further and pricing decision, made on evidence.
